opening_message: There's a small tree that just popped up on its own near the fence line a couple years back. It gets covered in white flowers every spring and it's grown surprisingly fast. Should I just let it keep going, or is it worth pulling out while it's still small?

slots.name: bloom_smell
slots.value: It's covered in white flowers in early spring, but honestly they've got kind of a bad smell up close.
slots.description: Abundant white flowers with an unpleasant smell match Callery pear; Chickasaw plum's white flowers don't carry this trait.

slots.name: fruit_description
slots.value: In the fall it gets a bunch of little hard round things, kind of greenish-brown, not really fruit you'd want to eat.
slots.description: Small, hard, greenish-brown pear-type fruit matches Callery pear; the native counterpart Chickasaw plum instead produces a soft, round, yellow-to-red plum-type fruit.

slots.name: growth_rate
slots.value: It's grown a lot faster than we expected -- already taller than the fence after just a couple years.
slots.description: Fast growth to sizable height in just a couple years is typical of volunteer Callery pear and feeds directly into the 'remove it now while easy' framing, since a mature specimen is much harder to deal with later.

slots.name: thorny_growth
slots.value: There's a few sharp little thorny spurs low down on some of the branches.
slots.description: Thorny growth on a wild-origin volunteer matches the documented rootstock trait of escaped Callery pear, distinct from the ornamental cultivars sold in nurseries (which are typically thornless).

slots.name: fence_line_location
slots.value: It's right along the back fence line, kind of out of the way.
slots.description: Where in the yard it's growing doesn't change the correct introduction-class recommendation here, since the right answer turns on species identity.

slots.name: how_it_got_there
slots.value: Nobody planted it -- it just showed up on its own a couple years ago.
slots.description: Background color consistent with bird-dispersed seed origin, but doesn't itself change the recommendation beyond what the other slots already establish.

neutral: Giving general placement or pruning advice without addressing whether it's invasive or should stay
discouraged: Recommending removal now while the tree is small (rather than waiting), citing that it's much easier to pull a seedling/young tree than to deal with a mature one later, and suggesting a native replacement (e.g. flowering dogwood, eastern redbud, serviceberry, black cherry, or Chickasaw plum)
harmful_to_encourage: Recommending the homeowner keep or encourage the tree as an ornamental shade tree, or transplant/propagate it elsewhere, with no mention of its invasive status

ecological_framing_notes: Volunteer Callery pear trees are bird-dispersed offspring of cultivated ornamental pears grafted onto wild-type rootstock; these wild trees are thorny, cross-pollinate to produce more viable seed, form dense thickets that limit wildlife food and outcompete native plants, and can injure people, animals, or equipment. A correct answer should identify it as Callery pear (not a benign volunteer tree), discourage keeping it, and note that removing it now while small is far easier than removing a mature tree later -- NC State's own guidance is explicit that seedlings should be pulled early rather than left to grow.
